theme: The Quran is a mercy sent on a blessed night, yet Makkah doubts it. The surah warns with the smoke, Pharaoh’s drowning and the Day of Sorting, then sets Hell’s zaqqūm beside Paradise’s gardens.
story: Revealed in Makkah, around the time of Az-Zukhruf and a little after it. Quraysh had grown more and more hostile, so the Prophet ﷺ prayed that they be struck with years of famine like the years of Yūsuf, hoping hardship would soften their hearts.

The famine was so severe they ate bones and dead animals, and a starving man looking up saw only a haze like smoke. Reportedly Abū Sufyān came asking the Prophet ﷺ to pray for rain. He prayed, rain came, and they went back to denial.

The surah answers them. The Quran is a mercy, not a calamity. Relief won’t change a stubborn heart, just as it didn’t change Pharaoh’s people. Everyone meets on the Day of Sorting, and the sinner and the righteous end up in very different places.

sections.title: The Quran came down on a blessed night as mercy from Allah
sections.meaning: Allah swears by the clear Book that He sent it down on a blessed night, to warn. On that night every firm matter is set out by His command. Sending messengers is a mercy from the Lord of the heavens and earth. There is no god but Him: He gives life and death.
points: By the clear Book: sent down on a blessed night, to warn
That night every firm matter is set out
A command from Us; messengers sent as mercy from your Lord
Lord of heavens and earth; no god but Him; gives life and death
sections.matters: It lays the surah’s base: the Quran is from Allah, sent on the best of nights, and it is a mercy. Its Sender is the Lord they already admit created everything, so He alone deserves worship.
sections.story: No specific incident. The blessed night is Laylat al-Qadr, in Ramadan. Some said it was the middle night of Shaʿbān, but the Quran itself says it was sent down in Ramadan (2:185).
explained: Ḥā Mīm opens the surah, and Allah swears by al-kitāb al-mubīn, the Book that makes things clear. He sent it down on a laylah mubārakah, a night full of blessing. The whole Quran came down to the lowest heaven that night, then reached the Prophet ﷺ in parts over the years. Its purpose: to warn.

On that night every amr ḥakīm, every firm matter, is set out: the year’s lifespans and provision are handed to the angels who record them. Sending messengers is raḥmah, a mercy from the Lord who hears and knows. He is Lord of the heavens and earth. If they were truly certain of that, they would worship Him alone.
teaches: Guidance through the Quran is the greatest mercy Allah gives.
Laylat al-Qadr is the night the year’s decrees are set out.
The One who creates and gives life is the only One to worship.
Following forefathers is no excuse for worshipping others.
sections.hook: Ayat 3 and 5 both end with innā kunnā: mundhirīn (warning), then mursilīn (sending). Ḥā Mīm and “the clear Book” are the same opening words as Az-Zukhruf just before it.

sections.title: Doubters, covered by smoke, beg relief, relapse, then face the greatest seizure
sections.meaning: The disbelievers play around in doubt. So watch for the Day the sky brings a visible smoke covering people. They cry, “Remove it, we believe!” But a clear Messenger already came, and they called him taught and mad. Allah will lift it a little; they will go back, until the Day of the greatest seizure.
points: They play around in doubt
Watch for the Day the sky brings a visible smoke
“Our Lord, remove the torment; we believe!”
A clear Messenger came; they called him taught and mad
Lifted briefly, they return; then the greatest seizure
sections.matters: It shows why hardship alone doesn’t change a stubborn heart. They already had a clear Messenger and turned away, so a promise made under pressure means little. And it warns that a far bigger blow is coming.
sections.story: Reportedly the famine: Quraysh saw only a smoky haze from hunger, then asked the Prophet ﷺ to pray for rain. He did, rain came, and they returned to denial. Others say the smoke is a sign still to come before the Hour.
explained: The disbelievers are fī shakk yalʿabūn: sunk in doubt, playing instead of taking the truth seriously. So watch for the Day the sky brings a dukhān mubīn, a visible smoke. Either it was the haze starving Quraysh saw, or it is a sign before the Hour, like a cold for the believer and far worse for the disbeliever.

They beg: “Our Lord, remove the torment, we will believe.” How can a reminder help now? A clear Messenger came, and they called him muʿallam, taught by some human, and majnūn, mad. Allah lifts it a little, and they go straight back. Then comes al-baṭshah al-kubrā, the greatest seizure: either Badr or the Day of Resurrection.
teaches: Faith declared only under pressure rarely lasts.
Don’t wait for disaster before taking the reminder.
When Allah lifts a hardship, that is a test of sincerity too.
Treating the truth as a game leaves a person in doubt.
sections.hook: Fa-rtaqib, “so watch”, opens the warning in ayah 10 and returns in ayah 59 to close the surah. “Remove the torment” (12) is answered with “We will remove the torment” (15).

sections.title: Mūsā calls Pharaoh’s people; they drown, leave gardens, and Israel is saved
sections.meaning: Before Quraysh, Allah tested Pharaoh’s people. Mūsā, a noble, trustworthy messenger, said: release Allah’s servants and don’t be arrogant against Him. They threatened him, so he prayed against a criminal people. He left by night, the sea stayed still, and they drowned. Their gardens passed to others, no one wept, and Israel was saved.
points: A noble messenger: release Allah’s servants; don’t be haughty
I seek refuge from your stoning; if not, leave me be
He calls his Lord; leave by night, leave the sea still
Gardens, springs, crops and comfort left to another people
Sky and earth did not weep for them
Israel saved from Pharaoh, chosen, and tested with signs
sections.matters: It is Quraysh’s own situation told through history: a noble messenger, clear proof, stubborn refusal, then ruin. Wealth and power couldn’t protect Pharaoh, and the people he enslaved inherited what he left behind.
sections.story: No specific incident. The story is placed here because Makkah’s leaders faced the same test as Pharaoh’s people: a noble messenger, clear signs, and a choice between believing and being destroyed.
explained: Allah tested Pharaoh’s people with a rasūl karīm, Mūsā. He told them to hand over Allah’s servants, the Children of Israel, and not to raise themselves against Allah, since he brought clear proof. They threatened him, so he sought refuge in Allah from being stoned, or insulted. If you won’t believe, he said, then leave me alone.

They did neither, so he called on his Lord: these are a criminal people. He was told to leave by night, knowing they’d be chased. After crossing he was told to leave the sea rahwan, still and parted, so the army would walk in and drown. Their gardens, springs, fine places and easy life all passed to others.

Neither sky nor earth wept for them. The sky weeps for a believer whose good deeds rose through it, and the earth for his place of prayer; they left neither, and got no delay. Israel was saved from humiliating torment, chosen over the people of their time, and given signs holding a clear trial, or a clear blessing.
teaches: Arrogance against Allah’s message ends in ruin, however strong a people are.
If people won’t accept the truth, ask them at least to leave you in peace.
Worldly comforts are on loan; Allah can pass them to others.
Good deeds leave a mark that the sky and earth miss.
sections.hook: The lost list runs gardens → springs → crops → fine places → comfort (25–27). “Gardens and springs” (25), left by Pharaoh’s people, return in ayah 52 for the righteous.

sections.title: Deniers want their forefathers back; creation isn’t play; Judgement Day gathers all
sections.meaning: The Makkan deniers say there is only the first death and dare the believers to bring their forefathers back. Are they better than the people of Tubbaʿ, destroyed for their crimes? Allah didn’t create the heavens and earth as play. The Day of Sorting is set for all, and only Allah’s mercy helps then.
points: Only our first death; bring back our forefathers
Better than the people of Tubbaʿ? They were destroyed
Heavens and earth not created in play, but in truth
The Day of Sorting: no relative helps, except through Allah’s mercy
sections.matters: It answers the denial underneath all the rest: no life after death. A world made with purpose must end in judgement, and resurrection comes on a set Day for everyone, not on demand. Only Allah’s mercy helps then.
sections.story: No specific incident. The Makkan idolaters argued that their dead forefathers had never come back, so there could be no resurrection. The people of Tubbaʿ, the kings of Himyar in Yemen, were a nation Quraysh knew well.
explained: They say: there is only our first death, and we won’t be raised. If you’re truthful, bring back our forefathers. But resurrection is for the Day of Judgement, not on request in this world. Are they stronger than the people of Tubbaʿ and the nations before them? Allah destroyed those people because they were criminals.

Allah didn’t make the heavens and earth as a game. He made them bil-ḥaqq, with truth and purpose: to be worshipped, and to reward and punish. Most people don’t realise it. So yawm al-faṣl, the Day of Sorting, is set for everyone, first and last. No mawlā, relative or friend, can help another, except those Allah has mercy on.
teaches: Resurrection comes at Allah’s appointed time, not at people’s demand.
Past nations were stronger than today’s deniers, and still fell.
A purposeful creation points to a Day of reward and punishment.
On that Day only Allah’s mercy helps, not family or friends.
sections.hook: Ayah 38 repeats “the heavens and earth and what is between them” from ayah 7. “Our first death” (35) returns in ayah 56: the righteous taste no death “except the first death”.

sections.title: The sinner eats zaqqūm, is dragged into Hell, and mocked as “mighty”
sections.meaning: The tree of zaqqūm is the sinner’s food. It boils in the belly like murky oil, like scalding water. He is seized, dragged into the middle of Hell, and scalding water is poured over his head. “Taste! You are the mighty, the noble!” This is what they used to doubt.
points: The tree of zaqqūm: food of the sinner
It boils in bellies like murky oil, like scalding water
Seize him, drag him, pour scalding water on his head
“Taste! You, the mighty and noble!” This is what you doubted
sections.matters: Once the Day of Sorting is named, this shows where the sinner ends up. It turns the arrogant man’s own boast back on him, and closes by naming the root problem: doubting what they were told.
sections.story: Reportedly ayah 49 is about Abū Jahl, who boasted that no one in Makkah’s valley was mightier or nobler than him. He was killed at Badr. The ayat still include every sinner like him.
explained: Zaqqūm is one of the foulest, bitterest trees, and it is the only food of al-athīm, the sinner. It is like al-muhl, the black dregs of oil, and it boils inside the belly like water at full boil. A single drop of it on earth would ruin life for everyone in the world.

The keepers of Hell are told: khudhūhu fa-ʿtilūhu, seize him and drag him roughly into the middle of the Fire, then pour scalding water over his head. Then, mocking him: “Taste! You are the mighty, the noble!” He thought his status would protect him; now he is the lowest. This is exactly what they used to doubt.
teaches: Status in this world protects no one from Allah’s punishment.
Arrogance here is answered with humiliation there.
What people doubt today becomes certain when they see it.
Take the warnings seriously now, while they can still help.
sections.hook: Two similes stand side by side: “like murky oil” (45) and “like the boiling of scalding water” (46). Al-ḥamīm appears in 46 and again in 48. Ayah 49 opens with one word: dhuq.

sections.title: The righteous rest safe in gardens; the Quran is easy, so watch
sections.meaning: The righteous are safe in gardens and springs, dressed in silk, facing each other, paired with ḥūr, calling for any fruit. They never die again and are kept from Hell: a bounty and the great success. The Quran is made easy in the Prophet’s ﷺ language, so watch; they are watching too.
points: A secure place: gardens, springs, silk, facing one another
Paired with ḥūr ʿīn; every fruit, in safety
No death but the first; saved from Hell; the great success
Made easy in your language; so watch, they’re watching
sections.matters: Paradise follows the Fire straight away, so both endings sit side by side. Then the surah closes where it began, with the Book, now described as easy to take in, and a final instruction to watch and wait.
sections.story: No specific incident. The closing “so watch” came before fighting was commanded: the Prophet ﷺ waits for Allah’s help, while the deniers wait for his downfall.
explained: The muttaqūn are in maqām amīn, a place safe from death, worry and ever leaving. Gardens and springs replace zaqqūm and scalding water. They wear sundus, fine silk, and istabraq, thick silk, and sit facing each other, no one’s back to another. They are paired with ḥūr ʿīn and call for any fruit, knowing it will never run out.

They never taste death there, apart from the first death in this world, and they are kept from the Fire. All of it is faḍl, a bounty from Allah, more than their deeds could earn. Finally, the Quran is made easy in the Prophet’s ﷺ language so they’ll take heed. So watch: they are watching too.
teaches: Those who feared Allah here will be safe from all fear there.
Paradise is Allah’s bounty, beyond what our deeds could earn.
The Quran is easy for anyone who truly seeks guidance from it.
Wait for Allah’s help patiently, whatever the deniers are waiting for.
sections.hook: The surah closes with fa-rtaqib (59), the same “so watch” as ayah 10. “Gardens and springs” (52) repeat ayah 25, and ayah 54 opens with kadhālik, “thus”, just like ayah 28.

groups.text: Ḥā Mīm. Allah swears by the Quran, the Book that makes things clear.
He sent it down on a blessed night, to warn: the night every firm matter of the year is set out.
It is His command. Sending messengers is a mercy from the Lord who hears and knows.
Lord of the heavens and earth, the only God, who gives life and death: your Lord and your forefathers’ Lord.
Yet they play in doubt. So watch for the Day the sky brings a visible smoke covering people: a painful torment.
They beg for relief and promise faith, though they already turned from a clear Messenger and called him taught and mad.
Allah lifts it a little and they return, until the Day of the greatest seizure.
Mūsā, a noble messenger, told Pharaoh’s people: release Allah’s servants and don’t be arrogant against Allah.
He sought refuge from their stoning, asked to be left alone, then called on his Lord against a criminal people.
Leave by night with My servants; you’ll be chased. Leave the sea still; they are an army to be drowned.
They left gardens, springs, crops and comfort to another people. Neither sky nor earth wept for them, and they got no delay.
Allah saved the Children of Israel from Pharaoh, chose them knowingly, and gave them signs holding a clear trial.
The Makkan deniers say there is only one death and no rising: bring back our forefathers.
Are they better than the people of Tubbaʿ and those before them? Allah destroyed them for their crimes.
Allah didn’t create the heavens and earth as play, but with truth. Most people don’t know.
The Day of Sorting is set for all. No relative helps then, except those Allah shows mercy.
The tree of zaqqūm is the sinner’s food, boiling in bellies like murky oil and scalding water.
Seize him, drag him into the middle of Hell, and pour scalding water over his head.
“Taste! You, the mighty, the noble!” This is what you used to doubt.
The righteous are in a safe place, among gardens and springs, dressed in silk, facing one another.
Paired with wide-eyed ḥūr, they call for any fruit, safe and secure.
No death after the first, and kept from Hell: a bounty from your Lord and the great success.
The Quran is made easy in your language so they’ll take heed. So watch; they are watching too.

1.explain: Ḥā Mīm: separate letters that open the surah. Only Allah knows what He means by them, but they were not sent without wisdom.

2.explain: Allah swears by al-kitāb al-mubīn, the clear Book: the Quran, which makes plain what people need, such as the lawful and the unlawful. It is an oath by the Quran about the Quran.

3.explain: Laylah mubārakah: a night full of blessing, Laylat al-Qadr, better than a thousand months. The best speech came down on the best night, to warn people. Some said the middle night of Shaʿbān, but Ramadan is correct.

4.explain: Yufraq: on that night every amr ḥakīm, every firm matter of the coming year, such as lifespans and provision, is set out and handed to the angels who write it. It will not be changed.

5.explain: Everything decreed, and every revelation, happens by Allah’s command. Innā kunnā mursilīn: He has always sent messengers, Muhammad ﷺ and those before him, to recite His clear signs to people.

6.explain: Sending messengers and books is raḥmah, a mercy from your Lord. As-Samīʿ al-ʿAlīm: He hears every voice, and He knows how badly people need guidance.

7.explain: He is Lord of the heavens, the earth and all between them, creating and running it all. If you are truly certain of that, then know He is the only true God.

8.explain: Lā ilāha illā Huwa: there is no god but Him. He alone gives life and death, and will gather you after death. He is your Lord and your first forefathers’ Lord, so their ways are no excuse.

9.explain: Despite all this clarity, they are fī shakk yalʿabūn: sunk in doubt about the Quran, mocking it and playing, distracted from what they were created for.

10.explain: Fa-rtaqib: so watch for the Day the sky brings a dukhān mubīn, a visible smoke. Either the haze the starving Quraysh saw, or a sign still to come before the Hour.
10.why: Quraysh grew stubborn, so the Prophet ﷺ prayed for years of famine like Yūsuf’s. They ate bones and dead animals, and a man looking at the sky saw only a smoky haze from hunger. Reportedly this ayah was then revealed.

11.explain: Yaghshā an-nās: it covers people, and they are told, or tell each other, “This is a painful torment.” If it was the famine, it hit Makkah; if a sign of the Hour, it covers everyone.

12.explain: They cry: “Our Lord, remove the torment; we are believers.” It is a promise made only because the punishment is on them. Reportedly Abū Sufyān came asking the Prophet ﷺ to pray for his dying people.

13.explain: Annā lahum adh-dhikrā: how can a reminder help them now? Faith declared when the punishment lands is no use, and a Messenger who made everything clear had already come to them.

14.explain: They turned away from him and said muʿallam, he is taught by some human, and majnūn, he is mad. They had already rejected the clearest reminder.

15.explain: Allah lifts the torment for a little while, and they return to disbelief. Or it means: even if sent back to the world, they would return to what they did before.
15.why: Reportedly the Prophet ﷺ was asked to pray for rain for Muḍar, who were dying. He prayed, rain came, and this ayah was revealed. Once life was easy again, they went back to their old ways.

16.explain: Al-baṭshah al-kubrā: the greatest seizure, when Allah takes vengeance. Either the Day of Badr, or the Day of Resurrection. Badr was also a day of vengeance.
16.why: When Quraysh went back to disbelief after the rain, this ayah was reportedly revealed, pointing to their defeat at Badr.

17.explain: Fatannā: before Quraysh, Allah tested Pharaoh’s people by sending them a rasūl karīm, a noble messenger: Mūsā, whom Allah spoke to.

18.explain: Addū ilayya ʿibād Allāh: hand over Allah’s servants, the Children of Israel, and free them from your torment. I am a trustworthy messenger, adding nothing and hiding nothing.

19.explain: Lā taʿlū ʿalā Allāh: don’t raise yourselves against Allah by refusing to worship Him or oppressing His servants. I bring sulṭān mubīn, clear proof: the miracles.

20.explain: They threatened to kill him, so he sought refuge in his Lord and theirs from being stoned: either with stones, or with insults such as calling him a sorcerer.

21.explain: If you won’t believe me, then leave me: neither with me nor against me. Faith was what he wanted; at the very least they could leave him in peace. They did neither.

22.explain: He called on his Lord: these are qawm mujrimūn, a criminal people. Simply describing their state was itself a prayer against them, and Allah answered it.

23.explain: Fa-asri bi-ʿibādī: leave with My servants, the Children of Israel, by night. Pharaoh and his people will chase you.

24.explain: Rahwan: after crossing, leave the sea still and parted, as it is. Mūsā wanted to strike it closed, but the army had to walk in and drown, so he had nothing to fear.

25.explain: Kam tarakū: how much they left behind after the drowning: gardens, and springs of flowing water.

26.explain: …and crops, and maqām karīm: fine dwellings and elevated, beautiful places.

27.explain: …and the soft, easy life they enjoyed, eating and wearing whatever they liked, with wealth and power in the land. All of it was taken in a single morning.

28.explain: Kadhālik: that is how it was. Allah passed their wealth to another people, the Children of Israel, whom they had enslaved.

29.explain: Neither sky nor earth wept for them: no good deeds rose from them, and no place of prayer on earth missed them. Nor were they given more time, even to repent.

30.explain: Allah saved the Children of Israel from al-ʿadhāb al-muhīn, the humiliating torment: their sons killed, their women kept alive, and hard forced labour.

31.explain: From Pharaoh: he was ʿāliyan, arrogant and self-exalting, and one of those who cross every limit Allah set.

32.explain: Ikhtarnāhum ʿalā ʿilm: Allah chose them knowingly, over the people of their own time, just as Maryam was chosen over the women of her time.

33.explain: He gave them signs, like the parting of the sea, and manna and quails. Balāʾ mubīn: either a clear blessing, or a clear test of who would be guided.

34.explain: Hāʾulāʾ, “these people”: the idolaters of Makkah really do say this. Their denial of the resurrection is quoted next.

35.explain: In hiya illā mawtatunā al-ūlā: there is only our first death, and we won’t be munsharīn, raised again. Just this life: no rising, no Paradise, no Fire.

36.explain: Bring back our forefathers, if you are truthful! A false argument: the resurrection is for the Day of Judgement, not on request in this world.

37.explain: Are they better, or stronger, than the people of Tubbaʿ, the kings of Himyar in Yemen, and the nations before? Allah destroyed them for their crimes. The blame falls on his people, not Tubbaʿ himself.

38.explain: Allah didn’t create the heavens, the earth and what is between them lāʿibīn, as play. He is far above pointless, foolish work.

39.explain: Bil-ḥaqq: created with truth and purpose, so that He is worshipped and people are rewarded and punished. Most don’t know, so they never reflect on creation.

40.explain: Yawm al-faṣl: the Day of Sorting, when Allah judges between all creation. It is mīqātuhum, the set appointment for all of them, the first and the last.

41.explain: No mawlā, relative or friend, can help another at all, and no help comes from outside to hold back Allah’s punishment.

42.explain: Except those Allah has mercy on: the believers, who may intercede for one another by His permission. Al-ʿAzīz: Mighty in punishing His enemies; ar-Raḥīm: Merciful to the believers.

43.explain: Shajarat az-zaqqūm: one of the foulest, bitterest trees, which Allah makes grow in Hell.

44.explain: Ṭaʿām al-athīm: it is the only food of the sinner, sinful in word and deed. Abū Jahl is included, but it is not only about him.

45.explain: Ka-l-muhl: like the black dregs of oil, or foul, stinking pus. It boils inside their bellies.

46.explain: …like al-ḥamīm, water boiling at its fiercest. A single drop of zaqqūm falling on earth would ruin life for everyone in the world.

47.explain: Khudhūhu fa-ʿtilūhu: the keepers of Hell are told to seize him and drag him roughly into sawāʾ al-jaḥīm, the very middle of the Fire.

48.explain: Then pour scalding water over his head, a torment that never leaves it. It melts through what is inside him.

49.explain: Dhuq: taste! You are the mighty, the noble! Said in mockery: he claimed he was too mighty to be punished and too honoured by Allah. Now he is the lowest.
49.why: Reportedly about Abū Jahl, who told the Prophet ﷺ: “Neither you nor your Lord can do anything to me. I am the mightiest and noblest in this valley.” He was killed at Badr.

50.explain: Inna hādhā: this is what you used to doubt, tamtarūn. Now it is certain, in front of their eyes.

51.explain: Al-muttaqūn: those who guarded against Allah’s anger by leaving sin and obeying. They are in maqām amīn, a place safe from death, leaving, worry and every harm.

52.explain: Among gardens and springs: the direct opposite of zaqqūm and scalding water. Everything in them is pure delight, with nothing to spoil it.

53.explain: They wear sundus, fine silk, and istabraq, thick silk. Mutaqābilīn: facing each other, no one with his back to another, their hearts at ease together.

54.explain: Kadhālik: so it will be. Allah pairs them with ḥūr ʿīn, fair companions with large, beautiful eyes, as an honour to them.

55.explain: They call for any fruit, known or never seen before, and it comes at once. Āminīn: safe from it running out, from any harm, and from ever leaving.

56.explain: They never taste death there. The only death is the first one, already tasted in this world. And He has protected them from the punishment of the Fire.

57.explain: Faḍlan min rabbik: all of it is a bounty from your Lord, who enabled their deeds and gave beyond them. That is al-fawz al-ʿaẓīm, the great success.

58.explain: Yassarnāhu bi-lisānik: Allah made the Quran easy in the Prophet’s ﷺ language, the clearest of tongues, easy to say and understand, so that they would take heed.

59.explain: Fa-rtaqib: so wait for Allah’s promised help. Innahum murtaqibūn: they are waiting for your downfall. This came before fighting was commanded.
